models.q: How can the movement of pollen help fruit and vegetable crops grow?
models.restate: The response explains how moving pollen helps some crops grow.
models.answer: When bees move pollen between flowers, plants can form fruits and vegetables such as apples and squash.
exp: Pollen clings to a bee while it travels among flowers, so the bee can carry it away from the first flower.
The source says apples and squash form only when pollen reaches their flowers, connecting pollen delivery to crop growth.
models.sum: Bee visits can connect pollen from one flower with the seed-making process that allows some crops to form.
models.bad: Bees help crops grow by carrying finished apples and squash back to their hives.

models.q: How does a honeybee's dance help the colony use food sources?
models.restate: The response describes how a honeybee's dance can help its colony use food sources.
models.answer: A dance communicates where flowers are, helping other bees locate food instead of searching without a direction.
exp: The dance pattern gives hive mates information about the location of flowers.
Nectar is the sugary liquid bees collect from flowers, so finding those flowers helps bees gather a food source used to make honey.
models.sum: By pointing other bees toward flowers, a dance helps the colony locate nectar for honey production.
models.bad: A honeybee's dance makes flowers produce nectar more quickly.

models.q: How do a honeybee's seasonal behaviors help it get through winter?
models.restate: The response considers how honeybee behavior changes with the season.
models.answer: Honeybees prepare to endure winter by storing honey as food and clustering together inside the hive to stay warm.
exp: Nectar collected during warmer periods can be turned into honey, leaving food that bees can use later.
Clustering and eating stored honey address two different winter needs: warmth and energy.
models.sum: Stored food and close clustering help honeybees meet the challenges of winter inside the hive.
models.bad: Honeybees survive winter by migrating to warmer regions after storing pollen in their wings.

models.q: Why can the work of many bees affect more flowers than the work of one bee?
models.restate: The response examines why a colony's many bees can affect numerous flowers.
models.answer: A colony can spread pollen broadly because thousands of bees search for food and an individual worker visits many flowers on a trip.
exp: The hive's large number of foraging bees means the pollen-carrying work is not limited to one worker.
Each worker can visit dozens of flowers during a trip, extending pollen movement across many flowers.
models.sum: Many foraging bees, each visiting many flowers, allow pollen to be carried across a broad area.
models.bad: A large hive affects more flowers because every bee carries a different kind of seed.

models.q: How can a small solar cell provide power to a calculator?
models.restate: The response explains how a small solar cell can provide power to a calculator.
models.answer: Light striking a solar cell produces electric current, and a small cell can supply enough power for some calculators to run without batteries.
exp: The cell changes incoming light into an electric current rather than needing a moving fuel source.
The source gives calculators as an example of a device that uses a tiny solar cell instead of batteries.
models.sum: A solar cell can turn light into current that powers a small device such as a calculator.
models.bad: A calculator's solar cell stores sunlight as heat until the user presses a key.

models.q: Why can rooftop panels be a practical choice for some buildings?
models.restate: The response considers why rooftop panels can be practical for a building.
models.answer: Rooftop panels use otherwise empty space, and their lack of moving parts lets them make electricity quietly with little repair.
exp: Placing panels on a roof makes use of an area that might otherwise do no work for the building.
With no moving parts, the panels avoid the noise and some of the repair needs associated with moving machinery.
models.sum: Rooftop placement and a simple, quiet design are two practical features of solar panels.
models.bad: Rooftop panels are practical because they make the building receive sunlight after dark.

models.q: What should a building consider when judging how steady solar electricity will be?
models.restate: The response examines what affects the steadiness of a building's solar electricity.
models.answer: A building should consider changing sunlight conditions, because a panel produces less electricity on a cloudy day than on a bright day.
exp: The same panel does not produce an identical amount in every weather condition; cloud cover can reduce its output.
Measuring output in watts gives engineers a way to describe and compare how much power the panel is producing.
models.sum: Solar output varies with conditions, and watt measurements help describe that changing production.
models.bad: A panel produces more electricity on cloudy days because clouds concentrate sunlight onto its cells.

models.q: What is one conclusion the source supports about solar panels while they are operating?
models.restate: The response evaluates a feature of solar panels during operation.
models.answer: During operation, panels can make electricity without burning fuel or producing smoke, while their simple design needs little repair.
exp: Not burning fuel describes what the panel does not release while it is generating electricity.
Having few moving parts supports the separate point that panels work quietly and need little repair.
models.sum: The source connects solar panels' operation with no fuel smoke and a low-maintenance design.
models.bad: Solar panels produce no environmental effects at any point, including when they are manufactured and removed.

models.q: How can water vapor in the air become rain?
models.restate: The response explains how water vapor in the air can become rain.
models.answer: Water vapor cools into droplets that form clouds; when cloud droplets join and grow heavy, they fall as precipitation.
exp: Cooling changes vapor back into tiny liquid droplets, which gather to form clouds.
As cloud droplets join and grow heavy, gravity brings them down as rain, snow, or hail.
models.sum: Cooling and droplet growth move water from vapor to clouds and then back to the ground.
models.bad: Rain forms when clouds freeze into solid rocks that fall to Earth.

models.q: How do oceans and plants provide different routes for water to enter the air?
models.restate: The response compares how oceans and plants add water vapor to the air.
models.answer: Water enters the air through evaporation from oceans and lakes and through vapor released by plants from their leaves.
exp: Sunlight warms surface water, allowing some liquid water to change into vapor.
Plants take in water through roots and release some of it through leaf openings, providing another route for vapor to enter the air.
models.sum: Surface-water evaporation and plant release both move water into the atmosphere.
models.bad: Plants create new water in their leaves, while the Sun changes ocean water into salt.

models.q: How can water's movement include both rapid surface flow and long-term storage?
models.restate: The response describes different time scales in water's movement.
models.answer: Water can move downhill toward rivers after rain, while some water soaks into soil and remains underground for many years.
exp: Runoff moves water along hillsides into streams and rivers, providing a route back toward the sea.
Groundwater stores some rain below the surface for a much longer period, so not every part of the cycle moves at the same speed.
models.sum: The water cycle includes fast surface movement as well as slower underground storage.
models.bad: All rain immediately reaches the ocean because soil cannot hold water underground.

models.q: How does the same cooling process help create both clouds and fog?
models.restate: The response connects cloud formation with fog near the ground.
models.answer: When water vapor cools into droplets, it can form clouds higher in the air or fog close to the ground.
exp: The passage explains that rising vapor cools and becomes tiny droplets that gather into clouds.
Fog uses the same change from vapor to droplets, but the droplets form near the ground rather than high in the sky.
models.sum: Clouds and fog both form when vapor cools into droplets, with their location making the visible result different.
models.bad: Fog is rain that has evaporated after reaching the ground and then freezes in place.

models.q: Why do the ends of an arch bridge need firm supports?
models.restate: The response explains why an arch bridge needs firm supports at its ends.
models.answer: An arch directs weight outward and downward, so firmly anchored abutments are needed to resist the force at each end.
exp: The curved shape carries weight toward the ends instead of leaving it unsupported in the middle.
The abutments must be anchored in solid ground or rock to hold against the forces the arch transfers to them.
models.sum: The arch carries weight to its ends, where firm abutments help support the bridge.
models.bad: The end supports are needed because arches send all bridge weight straight upward.

models.q: How can an arch bridge cross a river while limiting supports in the water?
models.restate: The response considers how an arch bridge can cross a river with few supports in the water.
models.answer: An arch can span a wide gap by transferring its weight toward anchored supports at the ends rather than relying on many supports in the river.
exp: The source says arches can cross wide rivers and valleys without placing many supports in the water.
That design depends on abutments at the ends being firmly anchored to the ground or solid rock.
models.sum: A wide arch span can reduce in-water supports when its end supports are secure.
models.bad: An arch crosses a river by floating on the water and moving with the current.

models.q: What changes as a stone arch bridge moves from construction to a completed structure?
models.restate: The response traces a change between building and using a stone arch bridge.
models.answer: A temporary frame first holds the stones in place; after the arch is complete, the curve transfers weight toward the end supports.
exp: During construction the incomplete stones need a wooden frame to stay in position.
Once the arch is complete, its curve directs weight outward and downward along the structure toward the ends.
models.sum: The temporary frame supports the stones during construction, and the finished arch carries its load to the ends.
models.bad: The wooden frame remains inside a completed stone arch and carries all of its weight permanently.

models.q: What evidence shows that the arch form can be built with more than one material?
models.restate: The response examines how arch construction uses different materials.
models.answer: The arch form is not limited to ancient stone: modern builders also shape steel or concrete into long, thin curves.
exp: The passage gives surviving Roman stone arches as evidence of earlier stone construction.
It also identifies steel and concrete as materials shaped into modern arch curves, showing the form continues across materials.
models.sum: Arch construction has used stone historically and steel or concrete in modern bridges.
models.bad: Modern bridges use steel because stone arches cannot remain standing for long.

models.q: How can a public library give students more than one way to learn?
models.restate: The response explains how a public library can support student learning in different ways.
models.answer: Students can borrow books and attend free programs such as reading hours or tutoring at a library.
exp: Borrowing lets a student use a book without paying to keep it permanently.
Programs such as tutoring provide direct learning support in addition to materials students read on their own.
models.sum: Books to borrow and free learning programs give students complementary ways to use a library.
models.bad: Libraries help students by requiring them to purchase every book they use.

models.q: Why can evening hours matter to people who work during the day?
models.restate: The response considers how evening library hours affect access for daytime workers.
models.answer: Later hours give people who are busy during the day another time to visit and use library resources.
exp: Staying open into the evening changes the hours when the building can be reached.
Computers and internet access support tasks such as job applications, making those later hours useful for working visitors.
models.sum: Evening access can connect daytime workers with library technology and services.
models.bad: Evening hours help workers because libraries complete job applications for every visitor.

models.q: How do librarians and study spaces support two different parts of research?
models.restate: The response compares guidance from librarians with the role of a study space.
models.answer: Librarians can help a visitor locate reliable information, while quiet rooms provide a place to concentrate on using it.
exp: Finding dependable sources is an information-selection task that librarians can teach visitors to perform.
A quiet study room addresses a different need by reducing distractions while someone reads or organizes information.
models.sum: Libraries can support research both by guiding source selection and by providing room to study.
models.bad: Librarians make every source reliable simply by placing it in a quiet room.

models.q: How can shared library books serve more readers than a privately kept copy?
models.restate: The response explains how sharing books changes their reach.
models.answer: A library can let many people use books it purchases, and borrowing allows each copy to reach different readers over time.
exp: The source says libraries share each purchased book with many different readers rather than assigning it to one owner.
Borrowing for a limited time allows a book to return and become available to someone else.
models.sum: Shared copies and borrowing let library books serve a wider group of readers.
models.bad: Shared books reach more readers because a single copy can be read by everyone at the same moment.

models.q: Why does a new moon look different from a full moon?
models.restate: The response compares the Moon's appearance at new moon and full moon.
models.answer: At new moon the lit side faces away from Earth, while at full moon observers see the whole lit side.
exp: The new moon is nearly invisible because the illuminated half points away from our view.
At full moon the lit half faces Earth, so the visible shape appears as a bright circle.
models.sum: The Moon's phase changes which portion of its sunlit half is visible from Earth.
models.bad: A full moon looks larger because the Moon creates extra light during that phase.

models.q: How does the Moon's changing position create a pattern people can observe?
models.restate: The response explains how the Moon's orbit produces an observable pattern.
models.answer: As the Moon moves around Earth, the portion of its sunlit half visible to observers changes in a recurring sequence.
exp: The Moon's position changes during its orbit, changing how much of its lit half observers can see.
People can track this recurring sequence of visible phases, which has been used to build calendars over time.
models.sum: The Moon's orbit produces a repeating pattern of visible phases that people can observe and track.
models.bad: People use Moon phases as a calendar because each phase permanently changes Earth's orbit.

models.q: How does the Moon's gravity connect it to changing ocean tides?
models.restate: The response connects lunar gravity with changes in ocean water.
models.answer: The Moon's gravitational pull on Earth's water is a main cause of tides rising and falling.
exp: The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's at its surface, but it still exerts a pull on water across Earth.
That pull shifts the distribution of ocean water, producing the tide changes described in the source.
models.sum: The source links the Moon's gravitational pull with the rising and falling of ocean tides.
models.bad: The Moon's gravity heats ocean water until it rises and falls like boiling liquid.

models.q: How are the Moon's orbit and visible phases related over time?
models.restate: The response examines how the Moon's orbit relates to its repeating appearance.
models.answer: As the Moon moves around Earth, our view of its sunlit half changes in a repeating sequence of phases.
exp: Half of the Moon remains lit, but its changing position alters how much of that half is visible from Earth.
The source gives the time for a full phase cycle, showing that the changing view repeats on a regular schedule.
models.sum: The Moon's orbit changes our view of its sunlit half and produces a recurring phase cycle.
models.bad: The Moon's phases happen because Earth casts a shadow on the Moon every night.

models.q: How do different cactus features help it conserve and collect water?
models.restate: The response compares how a cactus conserves water and collects it.
models.answer: Narrow spines reduce water loss, while wide, shallow roots quickly absorb rain near the surface.
exp: Compared with broad leaves, narrow spines lose much less water to dry air.
Wide shallow roots address the other side of the problem by collecting rain before it dries away.
models.sum: Cacti conserve water with narrow spines and collect brief rain with shallow, spreading roots.
models.bad: Cacti make rain in their stems and send it into the soil through their roots.

models.q: How do cactus spines help it survive in a dry environment?
models.restate: The response explains how cactus spines contribute to survival in dry conditions.
models.answer: Narrow spines lose less water than broad leaves, and they can also shade the plant and discourage some animals from eating it.
exp: Replacing broad leaves with narrow spines reduces the surface that loses water to dry air.
The same spines provide some shade and protection, giving them more than one useful role.
models.sum: Cactus spines help conserve water while also offering shade and protection.
models.bad: Spines help cacti by collecting large amounts of water from the desert wind.

models.q: What evidence supports the idea that cacti can be low-water plants for people?
models.restate: The response evaluates evidence about cacti's ability to live with little water.
models.answer: Some cacti survive long periods without rain, which helps explain why people can grow them in pots that need little watering.
exp: Surviving a year or more without rain shows that some cacti are adapted to long dry periods.
The source connects that low-water need to their use as houseplants that require little watering.
models.sum: A cactus's tolerance of dry periods makes it suitable for people seeking a low-water houseplant.
models.bad: Cacti need little watering because their pots produce water whenever the plant becomes dry.

models.q: How do different cactus features address separate desert challenges?
models.restate: The response compares different features that help a cactus in desert conditions.
models.answer: A cactus can conserve and store water with its spines and stem while its wide roots collect rain quickly when it arrives.
exp: Narrow spines reduce water loss compared with broad leaves, helping conserve water already in the plant.
Wide shallow roots solve a different problem by quickly absorbing water near the surface after rain.
models.sum: Water conservation and rapid collection work together to help a cactus manage scarce rainfall.
models.bad: Cacti survive by turning their spines into deep roots that reach underground rivers.

models.q: How can pushing farther from a fulcrum change the effort needed to pry with a crowbar?
models.restate: The response explains how a person's push relates to effort when using a crowbar.
models.answer: Pushing farther from the fulcrum can reduce the force needed to lift a load, although the hand must travel a longer distance.
exp: A crowbar lets a person push on its long end to pry a nail upward.
The source explains the tradeoff: a longer distance from the fulcrum lowers needed force but requires more hand movement.
models.sum: A crowbar's lever arm can reduce force while increasing the distance the hand moves.
models.bad: A crowbar lifts a nail because it makes the nail weigh less before the person touches it.

models.q: How can levers use different fulcrum positions for different tasks?
models.restate: The response compares how fulcrum position relates to a lever's use.
models.answer: A lever's fulcrum can be arranged to lift a load, as in a wheelbarrow, or placed between two sides to balance them, as in a seesaw.
exp: A wheelbarrow pivots around the wheel, allowing the person to carry only part of the load at the handles.
A seesaw's middle fulcrum lets two riders balance when their weights are equal.
models.sum: Changing where a lever pivots changes how it supports or balances a load.
models.bad: A wheelbarrow and a seesaw work because neither one has a fulcrum.

models.q: How does fulcrum placement affect the force-and-distance tradeoff of a lever?
models.restate: The response examines how fulcrum placement affects a lever's tradeoff.
models.answer: Placing a fulcrum near the load lets a smaller push farther away lift a heavy object, but the hand must move through a longer distance.
exp: A fulcrum near the load makes it possible for a push farther away to lift a heavy object.
The farther push reduces force but increases how far the hand travels, so the placement changes the balance between effort and movement.
models.sum: Fulcrum placement changes the balance between the force needed and the distance the hand travels.
models.bad: A lever reduces force by creating extra energy that was not present in the person or tool.

models.q: How do scissors and a crowbar show that levers can be adapted to different actions?
models.restate: The response compares two tools that use lever action for different purposes.
models.answer: Scissors use two joined levers to cut, while a crowbar uses a long bar and a pivot to pry a nail upward.
exp: The shared fulcrum in scissors connects two lever arms so their movement can act on material between them.
The crowbar's lever action instead transfers a push on its long end into a lifting action at a nail.
models.sum: Lever principles support different tool designs, from cutting with scissors to prying with a crowbar.
models.bad: Scissors and crowbars work because their metal blades attract the objects they move.

models.q: How can a rider make pedaling easier on a steep hill?
models.restate: The response explains how a rider can make pedaling easier on a hill.
models.answer: The rider can shift to a low gear, in which each pedal turn moves the bicycle a shorter distance and requires less effort.
exp: In a low gear the bike travels a shorter distance per pedal turn, which makes pedaling easier on a steep hill.
The rider changes gears by moving a lever that shifts the chain to another toothed wheel.
models.sum: Shifting to a low gear helps a rider pedal up a steep hill with less effort.
models.bad: A low gear makes each pedal turn move the bike farther up the hill.

models.q: Why might a rider select a high gear on flat ground?
models.restate: The response considers why a higher bicycle gear can suit flat ground.
models.answer: A high gear moves the bike farther with each pedal turn, which can help a rider reach a higher speed on flat ground.
exp: The high gear's longer travel for each pedal turn makes it useful when the ground is flat.
A suitable gear also helps the rider maintain a steady and comfortable pedaling pace.
models.sum: On flat ground, a high gear can increase distance per pedal turn while supporting a steady pace.
models.bad: A high gear is best on flat ground because it makes the bicycle stop moving between pedal turns.

models.q: How does having several gear combinations help a rider respond to changing conditions?
models.restate: The response explains why a range of gear combinations can be useful.
models.answer: A range of gears lets a rider choose shorter travel per pedal turn for a hill or longer travel on flat ground, adapting effort and speed to conditions.
exp: Many bicycles provide several gear combinations, giving a rider more than one fixed ratio to use.
The low-gear example shows how one choice reduces effort on a steep hill, demonstrating why different conditions call for different ratios.
models.sum: A range of gear choices gives riders flexibility to match pedaling to the terrain.
models.bad: More gear combinations make every gear equally easy on every kind of terrain.

models.q: How can a low gear support both easier pedaling and a comfortable pace on a hill?
models.restate: The response explains how a gear choice can affect effort and riding pace on a hill.
models.answer: A low gear shortens the distance moved per pedal turn, making a steep climb easier and helping the rider maintain a comfortable pace.
exp: The shorter travel per pedal turn in a low gear reduces how hard the rider must push on a steep hill.
Choosing an appropriate gear helps a rider keep a steady, comfortable pedaling pace rather than forcing one speed everywhere.
models.sum: A low gear can make climbing easier while helping a rider keep a steady pace.
models.bad: Low and high gears differ only in the color of the chain, not in how far the bicycle moves.

models.q: Why can rust make an iron object more likely to break?
models.restate: The response explains how rust affects an iron object's strength.
models.answer: Rust is weaker than iron, so an object can crumble or break when much of its iron surface has rusted.
exp: The reaction of iron with oxygen in the presence of water forms rust on the object.
Because rust is weaker than iron, a badly rusted object can lose strength and break apart.
models.sum: Rust forms on iron and is weaker than the metal, which can leave an object more likely to fail.
models.bad: Iron rusts faster in damp places because water removes all oxygen from the metal.

models.q: How can a gardener reduce rust on an iron tool after using it?
models.restate: The response describes a way to protect a garden tool from rust.
models.answer: The gardener can dry the tool and coat it with oil, creating a barrier that limits contact between iron, water, and air.
exp: Wiping the tool dry removes water left from use before it can take part in rust formation.
Painting keeps air and water away from iron; an oil coating serves the same protective purpose on a tool.
models.sum: Drying and coating an iron tool help keep the conditions for rust away from its surface.
models.bad: A gardener can stop rust by leaving a wet tool outside so the water washes the iron away.

models.q: What do stainless steel and paint have in common as rust-prevention methods?
models.restate: The response compares two ways of reducing rust.
models.answer: Both methods protect iron by limiting its exposure to conditions that cause rust, though stainless steel uses a chromium layer and paint covers the surface.
exp: Chromium in stainless steel forms a thin protective layer at the surface.
Paint acts as a covering that keeps air and water from reaching the iron underneath, achieving a related protective result by another method.
models.sum: Different surface barriers can protect iron from rust-producing exposure.
models.bad: Stainless steel and paint prevent rust by removing all iron from the object.

models.q: Why does the source distinguish iron-containing steel from gold when describing rust?
models.restate: The response examines how the materials in an object relate to rust.
models.answer: Steel is mostly iron and can rust, whereas the passage gives gold as an example of a metal that does not rust.
exp: Because steel contains mostly iron, it includes the metal involved in rust formation.
Gold provides a contrast: not every metal responds to rust in the same way as iron.
models.sum: Material composition matters because iron-containing steel and gold do not behave alike around rust.
models.bad: Steel cannot rust because adding any other material removes its iron.

models.q: How do a rover's wheels and cameras work together during exploration?
models.restate: The response explains how rover movement can support observation.
models.answer: Grooved wheels help a rover cross loose ground, while cameras let it study rocks from a distance.
exp: The grooves help the metal wheels grip loose sand and rocks so the rover can keep moving.
Once in position, cameras allow scientists to examine rocks without traveling to the rover themselves.
models.sum: Mobility across loose ground and onboard cameras help rovers reach and observe Martian features.
models.bad: Rover wheels photograph rocks by turning their grooves toward the surface.

models.q: How does the length of a Martian day affect the timing of rover work?
models.restate: The response considers how a Martian day shapes the timing of rover activity.
models.answer: A Martian day lasts slightly longer than an Earth day, and rovers often carry out instruction lists during the Martian day.
exp: The source gives the length of a Martian day as a little longer than a day on Earth.
Since rovers often perform instructions during that local day, mission teams must account for the different daily schedule.
models.sum: Rover operations follow a Martian day that is slightly longer than an Earth day.
models.bad: Engineers use a joystick because radio messages arrive before they are sent from Earth.

models.q: How can a rover turn a visit to a rock into useful information for scientists on Earth?
models.restate: The response traces how rover instruments produce information for scientists.
models.answer: A rover can use a drill or camera to examine a rock and send observations that scientists can study from Earth.
exp: Drills and cameras allow a rover to gather close information about rocks at its location.
Because radio messages travel with a delay, collected observations can be transmitted back for scientists to examine later rather than steering the rover moment by moment.
models.sum: Rover instruments collect local evidence that can be sent to Earth for later scientific study.
models.bad: Rovers teach scientists about rocks by bringing every sample back to Earth immediately.

models.q: How do rovers and a small helicopter represent different ways to explore another planet?
models.restate: The response compares two kinds of robotic exploration on another planet.
models.answer: Rovers travel across the surface on wheels, while the Ingenuity helicopter explored above the surface through powered flight.
exp: Grooved wheels are suited to gripping loose sand and rocks along the ground.
Ingenuity's powered flight provided a different way to explore by moving through the air rather than over the surface.
models.sum: Surface travel and powered flight give robotic missions different ways to examine another planet.
models.bad: The Ingenuity helicopter explored Mars by rolling across the ground on grooved wheels.

models.q: How could printers change the words in a new page without making new metal letters?
models.restate: The response explains how printers could prepare different words with reusable type.
models.answer: Printers could rearrange the same metal letters into a new frame for another page instead of making a new set of letters.
exp: Movable metal letters were the parts arranged to create printed words.
Because the type could be reused, printers could rearrange existing letters for a different page.
models.sum: Movable type let printers rearrange reusable letters to prepare different pages.
models.bad: Printers reused movable letters by melting each printed page back into metal.

models.q: How could lower book prices and new printing shops together widen access to books?
models.restate: The response considers how price and location affected access to books.
models.answer: Lower prices made books affordable to more people, and shops in many cities brought printing closer to readers.
exp: When printed books cost less than hand-copied ones, more people could afford to buy them.
As printing shops spread to more cities, readers could obtain books from more local places.
models.sum: More affordable books and more places to print them widened access for readers.
models.bad: Book prices fell because every printing shop gave all books away for free.

models.q: How did early printed books combine a new production method with a familiar visual style?
models.restate: The response examines how early printed books balanced production changes with appearance.
models.answer: Printers used movable type for production while early books often imitated the style of handwritten pages.
exp: Movable metal letters changed how text could be arranged and reproduced.
The copied handwritten appearance shows that a new production method did not require every visual feature of a book to change at once.
models.sum: Early printing changed how pages were produced while retaining familiar page styles.
models.bad: Early books looked handwritten because each copy was still written out by hand after printing.

models.q: How did the printing press depend on both a mechanical system and a suitable ink?
models.restate: The response explains how different components supported printing.
models.answer: A press adapted from screw presses applied mechanical force, while thick oil-based ink helped the metal letters leave marks on paper.
exp: The adapted screw-press design supplied a mechanism for pressing the arranged type against a surface.
The ink's thick, oily quality helped it stick to metal letters so it could be transferred in printing.
models.sum: Printing required both a mechanism to press type and ink suited to the metal letters.
models.bad: Oil-based ink supplied the mechanical force that moved the press screw.

models.q: How can coral reefs have value for both ocean life and visitors?
models.restate: The response compares ways coral reefs can matter to animals and people.
models.answer: Reefs support many ocean species, and they also attract people who visit to swim and snorkel.
exp: The source describes species that depend on reefs, showing an ecological role.
It also says many reefs attract visitors, providing a separate reason people value them.
models.sum: Reefs can be important habitats and places people visit to experience ocean life.
models.bad: Reefs support many species because they cover most of the ocean floor.

models.q: How does the reef structure provide a place for young fish to grow?
models.restate: The response explains how coral structure can support young fish.
models.answer: The branches of coral provide shelter where young fish can live until they are large enough for open water.
exp: The branching coral gives small fish spaces to shelter while they are young.
Those branches are part of a reef formed from coral skeletons that accumulate over time.
models.sum: Coral branches offer shelter that can help young fish grow before moving into open water.
models.bad: Reefs protect shores by pulling waves beneath the ocean floor.

models.q: How do algae and coral skeletons contribute different parts to reef growth?
models.restate: The response compares two contributions to reef development.
models.answer: Algae inside coral make food using sunlight, while coral builds hard skeletons that accumulate to form reef structure.
